title: Why Samples Miss the Truth
question: Why does a sample's average almost never equal the whole group's?
hook: Measure a thousand people from a million and your answer will probably still be a little off.
idea: A sample is only part of the population, so its statistics differ from the true values, and a larger sample generally shrinks that gap.

beats.prompt: You average the heights of 1,000 people chosen fairly from a population of one million. Will it match the average of all one million exactly?

choices.label: Yes, a fair pick always matches the whole group
choices.feedback: Fairness removes bias, but a thousand people are still only part of the population.

choices.label: Typically not; it will differ by some amount
No, a fair pick is always wildly off
choices.feedback: Fair samples are usually close; the gap is real but is not always huge.

beats.explain: The sample leaves out most people, so its average typically differs from the population's. That difference is the sampling error.

pairs: A statistic of the whole population
beats.explain: A sample's statistic is used to estimate the population's parameter, and the gap between them is the sampling error.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: I fairly pick three people twice and average their sleep each time.
The two averages come out very different from each other.
So the way I picked people must have been biased.
So I should trust averages from tiny samples less.
beats.explain: Even a perfect, unbiased sample has error from chance, and averaging two or three people gives wildly varying results each time.

beats.prompt: A team doubles its sample from 1,000 people to 2,000. What generally happens to the likely sampling error, and what is the catch?

choices.label: It generally shrinks, but the larger sample costs more
It drops to exactly zero at no extra cost
choices.feedback: Error shrinks but does not vanish, and surveying more people costs more.

choices.label: It grows, because more people means more mistakes
choices.feedback: A larger sample generally lowers the likely error.

beats.explain: A larger sample generally reduces the likely size of the error, but the cost of increasing it may be prohibitive.
